questions.q: How is a data migration different from a metadata migration in a Salesforce project?
options: Data migration moves actual record data; metadata migration moves configuration like objects, fields, and flows, usually via change sets or DX
There is no real difference — change sets handle both
Metadata migration only happens during cutover, while data migration happens during development
Data migration is only needed when moving away from Salesforce, never into it
questions.explain: Metadata migration carries configuration (objects, fields, flows, code) between orgs with built-in tools. Data migration carries the business's actual record data, which has no equivalent automated 'deploy' mechanism and requires its own planning.

questions.q: Put this course's three phases in the order they actually run.
options: Proving and Cutting Over, then Planning, then Designing the Migration
Designing the Migration, then Planning, then Proving and Cutting Over
Planning, then Designing the Migration, then Proving and Cutting Over
All three happen simultaneously, since they're independent workstreams
questions.explain: The course follows a real migration's shape: Planning (understand and scope), Designing the Migration (mappings, transformation, sequencing), then Proving and Cutting Over (validate, rehearse, go live).

questions.q: A project team decides to load data immediately with Data Loader, skipping source analysis and scope definition. According to this lesson, what is the most likely consequence?
options: Nothing — Data Loader is powerful enough to handle any data as-is
The load will simply fail to start until planning is complete
Salesforce will automatically flag the missing planning steps before allowing the load
Problems like duplicates and malformed records will still surface, just mid-load under time pressure instead of earlier when they're cheap to fix
questions.explain: Skipping planning doesn't make the underlying data problems disappear — it just delays discovering them until the worst possible time, during a live load instead of on a whiteboard.

questions.q: In a migration project, which decisions does this lesson say most clearly belong to the Technical Architect rather than being delegated to whoever runs the load job?
options: Which exact button in Data Loader's UI to click
Scope boundaries, object load sequencing, tooling choice, relationship/edge-case handling, and the rollback plan
Formatting the CSV files used for the load
Scheduling the calendar invite for the cutover meeting
questions.explain: The architect owns the decisions that are expensive to get wrong and hard to undo once a load starts — scope, sequencing, tooling fit, edge-case handling, and rollback — not the mechanical act of running the load.

questions.q: Which of these is listed in this lesson as a recurring, common root cause of real migration failures?
options: No rollback plan existing if a bad load needs to be undone
Using Salesforce DX to manage metadata deployments
Rehearsing the migration more than once before cutover
Defining scope precisely before building anything
questions.explain: The lesson lists no rollback plan as one of the recurring failure modes, alongside unprofiled source data, imprecise scope, wrong load sequencing, and no rehearsal — all planning or design failures rather than tooling failures.
